input:
A continuous stirred-tank reactor, or CSTR, is used to run a neutralisation reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant. For an ideal CSTR operating at steady state, the conversion that is achieved is governed by the product of the rate constant and the mean residence time, because the material balance on the limiting reactant is written over the whole vessel and the rate is evaluated at the outlet concentration, the contents of the vessel being uniform throughout as a consequence of the mixing.

In the present case, the rate constant is 0.073 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 50 min, which means that the product of the two quantities is 0.073 x 50 = 3.65, a dimensionless figure. The conversion is then obtained as this product divided by one plus the product, that is, 3.65 / 4.65 = 0.785, corresponding to a steady-state conversion of 78.5%. The reason the denominator takes this form is that the flowing stream continuously removes unreacted material from the vessel, so a CSTR converts less of its feed than a batch vessel that is held for the same length of time at the same rate constant.

It should be noted that this estimate rests on two important assumptions, namely perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is what permits the balance to be written in terms of a single outlet concentration, and a real vessel with stagnant zones or short-circuiting will tend to fall short of the ideal figure. Constant density, for its part, keeps the residence time as a property of the vessel and the flow alone. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been carried out, so neither assumption has yet been verified against the vessel's own behaviour, highlighting the fact that the conversion that has been calculated here is strictly the ideal-CSTR value for the stated conditions.

A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 78.5%. For an ideal CSTR at steady state with a first-order reaction, conversion is set by the product of the rate constant and the mean residence time: the product fixes the conversion through the balance on the limiting reactant over the vessel, in which the rate is evaluated at the outlet concentration because the vessel contents are uniform.

The rate constant is 0.073 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 50 min, so the product is 0.073 x 50 = 3.65, dimensionless. Conversion follows as the product divided by one plus the product: 3.65 / 4.65 = 0.785, the figure stated above as a percentage. The same product governs a plug-flow vessel differently, which is why the figure belongs to the stirred vessel and is not transferred to other reactor types that happen to share the rate constant and the residence time. The denominator exceeds the numerator by the unreacted share that the flowing stream removes from the vessel, which is why a CSTR at this product converts less of the feed than a batch vessel held for the same time at the same rate constant.

The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is what licenses the single outlet concentration in the balance; a vessel with stagnant zones or short-circuiting departs from it in the direction of lower conversion for the same residence time. Constant density keeps the residence time a property of the vessel and the flow alone. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so neither assumption has been checked against the vessel's own response, and the conversion figure stands as the ideal-CSTR value for the stated rate constant and residence time.
